10903.q: How can you tell the red-and-green macaw from the similarly red scarlet macaw?
a: Green instead of yellow wing coverts and red feather lines on the face
A completely blue head and yellow feet
A green breast and a black tail
A yellow eye ring like the hyacinth macaw
10903.e: The red-and-green macaw has green wing coverts with no yellow patch. Fine lines of tiny red feathers run across its pale facial skin.
10903.m: The red-and-green macaw has green wings and red lines on its face.

10904.q: Which species is the largest member of the genus Ara?
10904.e: The red-and-green macaw grows to around 90 to 95 cm long, making it the largest species of the genus Ara. Only the hyacinth macaw, from another genus, is longer.
10904.m: The red-and-green macaw is the largest macaw of the genus Ara.

10905.q: What colours is the blue-and-yellow macaw?
a: Blue on top, yellow on the breast and belly
Red with a yellow wing patch
Completely cobalt blue with a yellow eye ring
10905.e: The blue-and-yellow macaw is blue on its back, wings and tail and bright yellow to orange on its breast and belly. It is one of the best-known macaws in zoos.
10905.m: The blue-and-yellow macaw is blue on top and yellow underneath.

10906.q: Which is the only country in Central America where the blue-and-yellow macaw lives naturally?
10906.e: The blue-and-yellow macaw lives mainly in South America. In Central America, it is found only in Panama.
10906.m: In Central America, the blue-and-yellow macaw lives only in Panama.

10907.q: On which Caribbean island was the almost vanished blue-and-yellow macaw reintroduced with birds from Guyana around 1999 to 2003?
10907.e: On Trinidad, the blue-and-yellow macaw had been almost wiped out by the 1970s. With birds from Guyana, a population was established again in the Nariva Swamp.
10907.m: Thanks to reintroduction, blue-and-yellow macaws live on Trinidad again.

10908.q: In which country is the blue-throated macaw (Ara glaucogularis) endemic?
10908.e: The blue-throated macaw lives only in the Llanos de Moxos in the Beni department of Bolivia. It is considered critically endangered.
10908.m: The blue-throated macaw lives only in Bolivia.

10909.q: Where does the red-fronted macaw nest, since there are hardly any large trees in its dry habitat?
a: In abandoned woodpecker holes in cacti
10909.e: The red-fronted macaw lives in a semi-arid mountain region of Bolivia with cacti and thorn bushes. It breeds in crevices of vertical rock faces.
10909.m: The red-fronted macaw breeds in rock crevices.

10910.q: Why does deforestation in Costa Rica hit the great green macaw especially hard?
a: It depends heavily on one tree species for feeding and breeding
It can only breed in coffee plantations
It needs freshly cleared land to feed
It lives only in conifer forests
10910.e: In Costa Rica, during the breeding season the great green macaw eats mainly fruit of the almendro tree and usually nests in its holes. If this tree is cut down, it loses food and nesting site at the same time.
10910.m: The great green macaw needs the almendro tree.

10911.q: What is the smallest macaw species called?
10911.e: The red-shouldered macaw (Diopsittaca nobilis), also called the dwarf macaw, is the smallest macaw. It is hardly bigger than some parakeets.
10911.m: The red-shouldered macaw is the smallest of all macaws.

10912.q: Who is Lear's macaw named after?
a: The poet and painter Edward Lear
10912.e: Charles Lucien Bonaparte named the species after Edward Lear in 1856. The English poet and painter had earlier painted a very similar parrot.
10912.m: Lear's macaw honours the poet and painter Edward Lear.

10913.q: Where does Lear's macaw breed and sleep in Bahia (Brazil)?
a: In mangrove forests on the coast
10913.e: Lear's macaw lives in the dry Caatinga in north-eastern Bahia. It uses natural holes in sandstone rocks.
10913.m: Lear's macaw lives in sandstone cliffs.

10914.q: How has the population of Lear's macaw developed since the 1980s?
a: It has grown from around 60 to over 1600 birds
It has fallen from around 5000 to 60 birds
It has stayed completely unchanged since 1980
It has died out completely in the wild
10914.e: In 1983 only about 60 Lear's macaws were counted; by 2018 there were already around 1700. This is why the species was downgraded in 2009 from “critically endangered” to “endangered”.
10914.m: Thanks to protection, Lear's macaw has recovered strongly.

10915.q: Who is Spix's macaw named after?
a: The German naturalist Johann Baptist von Spix
10915.e: Johann Baptist von Spix collected the first specimen in Brazil in 1819. This is why the species bears his name.
10915.m: Spix's macaw honours the naturalist Johann Baptist von Spix.

10916.q: What IUCN status did Spix's macaw receive in 2019?
10916.e: After the last known wild Spix's macaw disappeared in 2000, the IUCN classed the species as extinct in the wild in 2019. It survived only in human care.
10916.m: Spix's macaw survived only thanks to captive breeding.

10917.q: What happened in 2022 in the conservation project for Spix's macaw in Bahia?
a: Captive-bred Spix's macaws were released into the wild for the first time
The last zoo bird of the species died
The species was discovered as a new species
All the birds were taken to Europe
10917.e: In June 2022, the first captive-bred Spix's macaws were released near Curaçá in Bahia. In 2023, chicks hatched in the wild there again for the first time.
10917.m: Since 2022, Spix's macaws have been flying in Brazil again.

10918.q: Which 2011 animated film made Spix's macaw famous around the world?
10918.e: In the film “Rio”, the two last Spix's macaws are the main characters. It drew a lot of attention to the endangered species.
10918.m: The film “Rio” tells the story of Spix's macaws.

10919.q: What happened to the Cuban macaw, which once lived on Cuba?
a: It died out in the 19th century
It was released back into the wild on Cuba in 2022
Today it lives only in Florida
10919.e: The Cuban macaw was last reliably recorded in 1864, when a bird was shot. Hunting, bird catching and habitat loss led to its extinction.
10919.m: The Cuban macaw died out back in the 19th century.

10920.q: Cockatoos form a family of their own. Which bird order does it belong to?
10920.e: Cockatoos form the family Cacatuidae within the parrots. They are set apart from the other parrot families, for example by their crest, which they can raise.
10920.m: Cockatoos are a family of their own within the parrots.

10921.q: Roughly how many species does the cockatoo family include?
10921.e: Depending on the classification, about 21 to 22 cockatoo species are recognised. This makes the family small compared with the other parrots.
10921.m: There are only around 21 cockatoo species.

10922.q: Which popular pet bird is a member of the cockatoo family?
10922.e: The cockatiel is a true cockatoo and is the only member of the subfamily Nymphicinae. Its crest, which it can raise, is typical. The budgerigar, on the other hand, belongs to a different parrot family.
10922.m: The cockatiel is a small cockatoo.

10923.q: Which language does the word “cockatoo” originally come from?
10923.e: The word goes back to the Malay “kakatua” and reached Europe in the 17th century via the Dutch “kaketoe”.
10923.m: The name cockatoo comes from the Malay word “kakatua”.

10924.q: Why are there no blue or green cockatoos, even though many other parrots have these colours?
a: Their feathers lack the fine structure that scatters blue light
Their food contains no blue pigment
Blue feathers would get too hot in Australia
10924.e: In parrots, blue and green are not made by pigments but by a special feather structure that scatters light (structural colour). Cockatoos lack it, which is why they are white, grey, pink or black.
10924.m: Cockatoos lack the feather structure for blue and green.

10925.q: Which feature do all cockatoo species have that sets them apart from most other parrots?
a: A crest of feathers they can raise
10925.e: All cockatoos have a movable crest of feathers. They raise it, for example, when landing or when excited.
10925.m: Every cockatoo can raise its crest.

10926.q: How are a cockatoo's toes arranged?
10926.e: Like all parrots, cockatoos have a climbing foot with two toes pointing forwards and two backwards. This arrangement is called zygodactyl and makes gripping easier.
10926.m: A cockatoo's foot has two toes in front and two behind.

10927.q: What are a cockatoo's powder down feathers for?
a: They produce a fine powder for the plumage
They produce scents for finding a mate
10927.e: Special down feathers break down into a fine powder, which the cockatoo spreads through its plumage while preening. It cares for the feathers and makes them water-repellent.
10927.m: Powder down gives the cockatoo a grooming powder for its plumage.

10928.q: In which area do cockatoos NOT live naturally?
10928.e: Cockatoos live in Australia, New Guinea, Indonesia, the Philippines and the Solomon Islands. On Borneo, however, there is not a single cockatoo species.
10928.m: Not a single wild cockatoo lives on Borneo.

10929.q: Where are roughly half of all cockatoo species found exclusively?
10929.e: Of around 21 species, 11 live only in Australia. This makes Australia the centre of cockatoo diversity.
10929.m: About half of the cockatoo species live only in Australia.

10930.q: Which cockatoo species is the smallest?
10930.e: The cockatiel measures only around 30 to 33 cm and weighs about 80 to 100 g. It is a true cockatoo.
10930.m: The cockatiel is the smallest of all cockatoos.

10931.q: What does “Nymphicus”, the genus name of the cockatiel, refer to?
10931.e: Early European travellers found the birds so beautiful that they named the genus after the nymphs of mythology.
10931.m: The cockatiel was named after the beautiful nymphs of legend.

10932.q: What does the species name “hollandicus” of the cockatiel mean?
a: It refers to New Holland, meaning Australia
It honours a Dutch zoo director
It shows that the species lives in Holland
It describes the orange colour of its cheeks
10932.e: “New Holland” was an earlier name for Australia. So the species name points to where the bird comes from.
10932.m: The name “hollandicus” recalls New Holland, the old name of Australia.

10933.q: How does the wild cockatiel behave in the dry regions of Australia?
a: It moves around as a nomad, following water and food
It lives in the same tree all year round
It migrates to New Guinea every year
10933.e: Cockatiels live mainly in dry regions and move to wherever there is water and seeds at the time. Hundreds can gather at one waterhole.
10933.m: Wild cockatiels follow water and food as nomads.

10934.q: How can you recognise an adult male in the grey wild-type cockatiel?
10934.e: Adult males have a bright yellow face and strong orange cheeks. Females have a greyer face and keep the bars across the tail.
10934.m: A yellow face gives away the male cockatiel.

10935.q: Which cockatoo, at around 55 to 60 cm long and weighing up to about 1.2 kg, is often considered the largest species?
10935.e: The palm cockatoo from New Guinea and northern Australia reaches around 55 to 60 cm and about 0.9 to 1.2 kg. Large yellow-tailed black cockatoos and sulphur-crested cockatoos can grow to a similar size.
10935.m: The palm cockatoo is one of the giants among cockatoos.

10936.q: What special behaviour do male palm cockatoos show?
a: They drum on wood with a stick
They build bowers out of blue objects
They dive for mussels in the sea
10936.e: Male palm cockatoos drum on dead branches with a stick they have shaped themselves or with a seed pod. The sound can be heard up to about 100 m away and is probably used to mark territory and attract a mate.
10936.m: The palm cockatoo is a drummer with a home-made drumstick.

10937.q: Roughly how often does a pair of palm cockatoos breed, and how many eggs do they lay?
a: One egg about every two years
10937.e: Palm cockatoos lay only one egg, and usually only every other year. This is one of the lowest breeding rates of all parrots.

10938.q: What is special about the palm cockatoo's red cheek patch?
a: It changes colour when the bird is excited
10938.e: The palm cockatoo has bare, red cheek skin. When it is excited or alarmed, its colour changes, so it is also used for communication.
10938.m: The palm cockatoo's cheeks show its mood.

10939.q: What is the threat status of the palm cockatoo on the IUCN Red List?
10939.e: The IUCN classes the palm cockatoo as “Near Threatened”. In Australia, it has even been considered vulnerable since 2015.
10939.m: The palm cockatoo is near threatened.

10940.q: What is the IUCN status of the yellow-crested cockatoo (Cacatua sulphurea)?
10940.e: The yellow-crested cockatoo is considered “Critically Endangered”. There are probably fewer than 2500 birds in the wild.
10940.m: The yellow-crested cockatoo is on the brink of extinction.

10941.q: What is the main cause of the sharp decline of the yellow-crested cockatoo in Indonesia?
a: Illegal capture for the bird trade
A fungal disease of the eggs
Hunting for its feathers for hats
10941.e: Above all, illegal capture for the cage bird trade has wiped out much of the population. On top of that comes deforestation, for example of mangroves and kapok trees.
10941.m: The bird trade has almost wiped out the yellow-crested cockatoo.

10942.q: In which big city lives a feral population of the yellow-crested cockatoo that makes up around 10 per cent of the world's wild population?
10942.e: An estimated 200 or so feral yellow-crested cockatoos live in Hong Kong. That is roughly a tenth of all the species' birds living in the wild.
10942.m: Of all places, Hong Kong is a refuge for the yellow-crested cockatoo.

10943.q: Which cockatoo from the island of Sumba was split off from the yellow-crested cockatoo as a separate species in 2023?
10943.e: The citron-crested cockatoo, with its orange crest, was long considered a subspecies of the yellow-crested cockatoo. Since 2023, it has been listed as a separate species.
10943.m: The citron-crested cockatoo from Sumba has been a separate species since 2023.

10944.q: In the sulphur-crested cockatoo, what does at least one bird do while the flock is feeding on the ground?
a: It keeps watch as a lookout
It collects food for the others
10944.e: At least one bird sits high up, often on a dead tree, and warns of enemies. That is why in Australia “cockatoo” even became a slang word for a lookout.
10944.m: In sulphur-crested cockatoos, one bird always keeps watch.

10945.q: Which new habit of sulphur-crested cockatoos in Sydney was described in a study in the journal Science in 2021?
10945.e: Cockatoos in Sydney lift the lids of wheelie bins to get at food scraps. The study showed that this technique spreads from suburb to suburb through social learning.
10945.m: Sydney's cockatoos learn to open wheelie bins from each other.

10946.q: What did research on the cockatoo “Snowball” show in 2009?
a: He can move to the beat of music
He recognises himself in a mirror
10946.e: Snowball, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, matched his dance moves to the beat of the music. The study in Current Biology showed that animals can also keep to a rhythm.
10946.m: Snowball the cockatoo proved that birds can dance to a beat.

10947.q: In which countries outside its natural range has the sulphur-crested cockatoo settled?
10947.e: Escaped or released sulphur-crested cockatoos have founded populations in New Zealand, Singapore and Palau, among other places.
10947.m: Sulphur-crested cockatoos now also live in New Zealand and Singapore.

10948.q: What is special about the genus Eolophus, to which the galah belongs?
a: It contains only this one species
It is known only from fossils
10948.e: The genus Eolophus is monotypic, so the galah (Eolophus roseicapilla) is its only member.
10948.m: The galah is the only member of its genus.

10949.q: Where does the name “galah” for this pink and grey cockatoo come from?
10949.e: “Galah” comes from “gilaa”, a word from Yuwaalaraay and related Aboriginal languages in north-western New South Wales.
10949.m: The name “galah” comes from an Aboriginal language.

10950.q: In Australian slang, what does “galah” mean when you say it to a person?
10950.e: In Australian slang, “galah” is an insulting word for a fool or idiot. It probably refers to the birds' loud, playful behaviour.
10950.m: In Australia, “galah” is a mocking word for a fool.

10951.q: How can you often tell the sex of a galah or Major Mitchell's cockatoo?
a: By the colour of the iris
By the length of the crest
By the colour of the feet
By the shape of the tail
10951.e: Males of all cockatoo species have a dark brown, almost black iris. Female galahs and Major Mitchell's cockatoos, however, have a pink to reddish iris.
10951.m: In many cockatoos, eye colour reveals the sex.

10952.q: How old was “Cookie”, a Major Mitchell's cockatoo at Brookfield Zoo near Chicago, whom Guinness World Records listed as the world's oldest living parrot?
10952.e: Cookie hatched in 1933 and died in 2016, so he lived to 83. He was considered the oldest Major Mitchell's cockatoo in captivity.
10952.m: Cookie the cockatoo reached the grand old age of 83.

10953.q: How is the work of incubating shared in black cockatoos?
a: The female incubates alone and the male feeds her
The eggs are hatched in the sand
10953.e: In black cockatoos, only the female sits on the eggs. The male brings her food several times a day; in the other cockatoos, both partners incubate.
10953.m: In black cockatoos, the mother incubates and the father brings the food.

10954.q: Where exclusively does the endangered Carnaby's black cockatoo live?
a: In the south-west of Western Australia
In the north of New Guinea
10954.e: Carnaby's black cockatoo is endemic to the south-west of Western Australia. The IUCN lists it as “Endangered”.
10954.m: Carnaby's black cockatoo lives only in south-western Australia.

10955.q: Roughly how long does the female Carnaby's black cockatoo incubate her eggs?
10955.e: At 28 to 29 days, Carnaby's black cockatoo has one of the longest incubation periods among cockatoos. In the cockatiel it is only around 20 days.
10955.m: Carnaby's black cockatoo incubates for almost a whole month.

10956.q: On which Philippine island is the most important stronghold of the critically endangered Philippine cockatoo?
10956.e: Palawan, especially the small island of Rasa, is the most important refuge. The Katala Foundation has protected the species there since 1998.
10956.m: The Philippine cockatoo has its stronghold on Palawan.

10957.q: According to the IUCN estimate, how many adult Philippine cockatoos still live in the wild?
10957.e: The IUCN estimates the population at around 430 to 750 mature birds. This is why the species is considered critically endangered.
10957.m: Only a few hundred adult Philippine cockatoos remain.

10958.q: Which feature does the male gang-gang cockatoo have?
10958.e: The otherwise grey male gang-gang cockatoo has a bright red head and crest. The female has a grey head, so there is a clear difference between the sexes.
10958.m: Male gang-gang cockatoos wear a red head.

10959.q: For which Australian region is the gang-gang cockatoo the official animal emblem?
10959.e: The gang-gang cockatoo is the faunal emblem of the Australian Capital Territory around Canberra. Its call is compared to a creaking gate.
10959.m: The gang-gang cockatoo is the animal emblem of the region around Canberra.

10960.q: What does the glossy black cockatoo mainly feed on?
10960.e: The glossy black cockatoo is a specialist in the seeds of she-oaks (Allocasuarina). It holds the cone in its foot, takes it apart with its bill and gets the seeds out.
10960.m: The glossy black cockatoo lives almost only on she-oak seeds.

10961.q: What is the IUCN status of the salmon-crested cockatoo from the island of Seram?
10961.e: The salmon-crested cockatoo is endemic to the Seram archipelago and is classed by the IUCN as “Endangered”. At up to 52 cm, it is one of the largest white cockatoos.
10961.m: The salmon-crested cockatoo from Seram is endangered.

10962.q: Where does the white cockatoo get its other English name, “umbrella cockatoo”?
a: From its crest, which it can raise into a semicircle
From sheltering its young under its wings
From its favourite tree with an umbrella-shaped crown
From its call, which sounds like rain
10962.e: When the white cockatoo is startled, it raises its white crest into a semicircle that looks like an open umbrella. The species lives on Halmahera and neighbouring islands and is considered endangered.
10962.m: The white cockatoo opens its crest like an umbrella.

10963.q: What did Goffin's cockatoo “Figaro” at the University of Vienna become known for in 2012?
a: He made his own tools out of wood
He learned to repair door locks
10963.e: Figaro bit splinters off wooden strips into the right shape to fish food out of a grid with them. Until then, this had not been known in cockatoos.
10963.m: Figaro the Goffin's cockatoo made his own tool.

10964.q: What did a 2023 study show about Goffin's cockatoos and tools?
a: They can carry several tools along as a set
They use stones to crack nuts in the sea
They throw sticks at enemies on purpose
10964.e: Goffin's cockatoos carried two matching tools together when a task needed both. Until then, a tool set like this was known mainly from chimpanzees.
10964.m: Goffin's cockatoos can use whole tool sets.

10965.q: Where was the only truly old cockatoo fossil found so far, from the early Miocene, discovered?
a: In the Messel Pit in Germany
In amber from the Dominican Republic
In the Gobi Desert in Mongolia
10965.e: A Cacatua fossil around 16 to 23 million years old comes from the Riversleigh fossil sites in Queensland. No other old cockatoo fossils are known.
10965.m: The oldest cockatoo fossil comes from Riversleigh in Australia.

10966.q: Which cockatoo species has officially been declared a pest in Western Australia?
10966.e: The little corella causes damage to fields and buildings in Western Australia. It was declared a pest there.
10966.m: In Western Australia, the little corella is considered a pest.

10967.e: Cockatoos do not build open nests but breed in holes in old trees, which they line with wood chips. The loss of old trees with holes therefore threatens many species.
10967.m: Cockatoos need old trees with nesting holes.

10968.q: What does a cockatoo usually show when it suddenly raises its crest?
a: That it is about to fall asleep
10968.e: Cockatoos raise their crest when they are excited, curious or alarmed, for example when in danger or as a greeting. At rest, the crest lies flat on the head.
10968.m: A raised crest shows that a cockatoo is excited.

10969.q: What age do larger cockatoo species typically reach in captivity?
10969.e: Large cockatoos often live 30 to 70 years in captivity. So anyone who keeps a cockatoo takes on a responsibility for decades.
10969.m: A large cockatoo can be a companion for a whole human lifetime.

10970.q: Which group of birds does the kiwi belong to?
10970.e: The kiwi belongs to the flightless ratites within the palaeognaths. It is the smallest living member of this group.
10970.m: The kiwi is the smallest living ratite.

10971.q: What does Apteryx, the kiwi's genus name, mean?
10971.e: Apteryx comes from Ancient Greek and means “without wings”. The name refers to the tiny wings hidden in the feathers.

10972.q: What do New Zealanders informally call themselves?
10972.e: The kiwi is New Zealand's national symbol, which is why people there call themselves “Kiwis”. “Aussies” is what Australians are called.
10972.m: New Zealanders call themselves “Kiwis” after their national bird.

10973.q: How many living species of kiwi are recognised?
10973.e: Today five kiwi species are recognised, including the North Island brown kiwi, the rowi and the little spotted kiwi. There is also one fossil species.
10973.m: There are five kiwi species today.

10974.q: According to DNA studies, which bird is the kiwi's closest relative?
a: The extinct elephant bird of Madagascar
The extinct moa of New Zealand
10974.e: Comparisons of DNA showed that the kiwi is most closely related not to the moa but to the elephant bird from Madagascar. So its ancestors must have flown to New Zealand.
10974.m: The kiwi's closest relative lived on Madagascar.

10975.q: Which anatomical feature does the kiwi have as the only bird in the world?
a: Nostrils at the tip of its bill
10975.e: In the kiwi, the nostrils are right at the front, at the tip of the long bill. This lets it smell prey in the ground.
10975.m: The kiwi smells with the tip of its bill.

10976.q: Roughly what is the kiwi's body temperature?
10976.e: Most birds have 39 to 42 °C. At around 38 °C, the kiwi is closer to a mammal.
10976.m: The kiwi has almost the body temperature of a mammal.

10977.q: What is unusual about the kiwi's bones for a bird?
a: The bones contain marrow instead of air
Its skull is made of cartilage
10977.e: Flying birds usually have hollow, air-filled bones. The kiwi's bones, on the other hand, contain bone marrow, as in mammals.
10977.m: Kiwi bones are filled with marrow.

10978.q: Why do the kiwi's feathers look like hair?
a: They lack the tiny hooks that link the barbs
They are made of a different keratin from other birds' feathers
They are greased with oil every day
They are hollow and branched inside
10978.e: Kiwi feathers lack the hooked barbules that, in other birds, link the barbs into a firm vane. That is why the plumage looks loose and fur-like.
10978.m: Kiwi feathers have no hooks and so look like fur.

10979.q: What does the kiwi's breastbone lack compared with flying birds?
a: The keel where the flight muscles attach
The wishbone as part of the breastbone
10979.e: Flying birds have a keel on their breastbone where the large flight muscles attach. The kiwi needs no flight muscles and therefore has no keel.
10979.m: Without flight, the kiwi needs no keel on its breastbone.

10980.q: Which gland, used by almost all birds to care for their feathers, does the kiwi not have?
10980.e: Most birds grease their plumage with the secretion of the preen gland. The kiwi lacks this gland, just as it lacks a tail.
10980.m: The kiwi has no preen gland.

10981.q: What is special about the egg-producing organs of the female kiwi?
a: It has no oviduct at all
It lays only eggs without a shell
10981.e: In most female birds, only the left ovary works. Female kiwis are among the few birds with two working ovaries.
10981.m: Female kiwis have two active ovaries.

10982.q: What is true of the kiwi's eyes compared with those of other birds?
a: Relative to body mass they are the smallest
Relative to body mass they are the largest
They face forwards like an owl's
10982.e: Relative to its body mass, the kiwi has the smallest eyes of all birds. It relies mainly on smell and touch; some wild kiwis are even blind.
10982.m: The kiwi sees poorly and has tiny eyes.

10983.q: How heavy can a kiwi egg be compared with the female's body weight?
10983.e: A kiwi egg can reach around a fifth of the mother's body weight. This is one of the largest eggs relative to body size among birds.
10983.m: A kiwi egg weighs up to a fifth of the mother.

10984.q: Roughly how many times heavier than a hen's egg can a brown kiwi egg be?
10984.e: A brown kiwi egg can weigh up to around 450 g. That is about six times as much as a hen's egg, even though the kiwi is hardly bigger than a chicken.
10984.m: A kiwi egg weighs as much as six hen's eggs.

10985.q: Who incubates the eggs in most kiwi species?
10985.e: In most kiwi species, the male does the incubating. Only in the great spotted kiwi and the rowi do the females help too.
10985.m: In kiwis, it is mostly the father who incubates.

10986.q: How many eggs does a kiwi clutch usually contain?
10986.e: A female kiwi usually lays only a single huge egg; sometimes a second one follows. With eggs this big, a larger clutch is hardly possible.
10986.m: A kiwi clutch usually consists of a single egg.

10987.q: Roughly how long is the kiwi's incubation period?
10987.e: Depending on the species and conditions, incubation lasts about 63 to 92 days. That is very long for a bird of this size.
10987.m: A kiwi egg is incubated for two to three months.

10988.q: What does a newly hatched kiwi chick live on in its first days?
a: The yolk store from the egg
10988.e: The chick hatches with a large yolk sac, which feeds it for about two and a half weeks. The parents do not feed it.
10988.m: A kiwi chick lives on its egg yolk at first.

10989.q: How long can a pair of kiwis stay together?
10989.e: Kiwis usually live in pairs, and a pair can stay together for up to around 20 years. During the breeding season, the partners meet in the burrow about every three days.
10989.m: Kiwi pairs often stay together for many years.

10990.q: Which kiwi species is the largest?
10990.e: The great spotted kiwi grows up to around 50 cm tall, and females weigh up to about 3.3 kg. This makes it the largest kiwi species.
10990.m: The great spotted kiwi is the largest kiwi.

10991.q: Which kiwi species is the smallest?
10991.e: The little spotted kiwi is the smallest kiwi species. Females usually weigh only about 1 to 2 kg.
10991.m: The little spotted kiwi is the smallest kiwi.

10992.q: Why are endangered kiwis deliberately settled on offshore islands?
a: There are no introduced predators such as stoats there
It is much warmer there in winter
They learn to fly more easily there
10992.e: Many small islands off New Zealand are free of stoats, cats and rats. Kiwis can grow up there undisturbed; this is how the little spotted kiwi was saved, for example.
10992.m: Predator-free islands are safe refuges for kiwis.

10993.q: Why was the rowi only recognised as a separate kiwi species in 2003, even though it had been known for a long time?
a: Only DNA comparisons showed the differences from similar kiwis
Until then it had lived only in zoos
It had previously been mistaken for a mammal
It had only just come about through cross-breeding
10993.e: From the outside, the rowi looks very similar to other kiwis. Genetic studies showed, however, that it is a separate species.
10993.m: Some species can only be recognised through DNA comparisons.

10994.q: On which main island of New Zealand do most kiwi species live naturally?
10994.e: The rowi, the southern brown kiwi and the great spotted kiwi live on the South Island. On the North Island, only the North Island brown kiwi lives naturally. Tasmania belongs to Australia.
10994.m: Most kiwi species live on New Zealand's South Island.

10995.q: What does the kiwi bird have to do with the kiwi fruit?
a: The fruit was named after the bird for export
The bird eats almost only this fruit
The fruit originally comes from New Zealand
The bird spreads its seeds in the forest
10995.e: The fruit comes from China and used to be called the Chinese gooseberry. Around 1959, New Zealand exporters renamed it after the brown, furry national bird.
10995.m: The kiwi fruit is named after the bird.

10996.q: Why did the kiwi probably lose the ability to fly in the course of evolution?
a: New Zealand had no predatory mammals on the ground, so flying was no longer worth it
A disease made its wings shrink
It is too windy in New Zealand to fly
10996.e: Before humans arrived, almost no mammals lived in New Zealand. With no enemies on the ground, flying was unnecessary for many birds, and they lost this ability.
10996.m: With no predatory mammals on the ground, the kiwi became flightless.

10997.q: Which extinct giant bird once lived in New Zealand like the kiwi?
10997.e: The moas were huge flightless birds of New Zealand and were wiped out after humans arrived. The dodo lived on Mauritius, the elephant bird on Madagascar and the great auk in the North Atlantic.
10997.m: The moa was a giant bird of New Zealand.

10998.q: What did the Māori traditionally use kiwi feathers for especially?
10998.e: The Māori made precious cloaks from kiwi feathers, the “kahu kiwi”. They were worn by respected people and are still regarded as treasures today.
10998.m: Valuable Māori cloaks were made from kiwi feathers.

10999.q: Roughly how many kiwis are estimated to still live in the whole of New Zealand?
10999.e: According to estimates, around 70,000 kiwis of all species still live today. In the past there were probably several million.
10999.m: Around 70,000 kiwis still live in New Zealand.

11000.q: How do the night-time calls of male and female kiwis differ?
a: Males call high and shrill, females deeper and hoarse
Only the females call, males are silent
Males call only during the day
11000.e: Male kiwis make shrill, whistling calls; the females call more deeply and roughly. Pairs often answer each other in the night.
11000.m: Male kiwis whistle high, females call low.

11001.q: What helps the great spotted kiwi survive in New Zealand's cool mountain areas?
a: Its thick, fur-like plumage insulates well
It migrates to Australia in winter
It warms itself in hot springs
11001.e: The kiwi's loose, hair-like plumage holds body heat well. This lets the great spotted kiwi cope even in the harsh mountain areas where it mostly lives.
11001.m: The fur-like plumage keeps the kiwi warm.

11002.q: What is the IUCN status of the little spotted kiwi?
11002.e: The little spotted kiwi is considered near threatened, and its population is growing. The other four kiwi species are considered threatened.
11002.m: The little spotted kiwi is only near threatened.

11003.q: What is the IUCN status of the North Island brown kiwi?
11003.e: The North Island brown kiwi is the most common kiwi species, but the IUCN considers it vulnerable. Without conservation measures, only a few chicks survive.
11003.m: Even the most common kiwi is considered vulnerable.

11004.q: Which introduced predator causes around half of kiwi chick deaths in many areas?
11004.e: Stoats were introduced to New Zealand and are responsible for about half of the kiwi chicks killed. Foxes and raccoons do not live wild in New Zealand.
11004.m: The stoat is the kiwi chicks' biggest enemy.

11005.q: Which animals are the greatest danger to adult kiwis?
11005.e: Adult kiwis can usually defend themselves against stoats, but not against dogs. A single dog running loose can kill many kiwis.
11005.m: For adult kiwis, dogs are the most dangerous.

11006.q: At roughly what weight are kiwi chicks big enough to defend themselves against stoats?
11006.e: Until they weigh about 1 to 1.2 kg, young kiwis are easy prey for stoats. After that, they are largely safe from them.
11006.m: From about a kilo, a young kiwi is safe from stoats.

11007.q: Without conservation measures, roughly what percentage of wild kiwi chicks reach adulthood?
11007.e: Without controlling the introduced predators, only about 5 to 10 per cent of chicks survive across the country. Most are eaten in their first months.
11007.m: Without protection, only about one in ten to twenty kiwi chicks survives.

11008.q: What happens in New Zealand's kiwi conservation programme “Operation Nest Egg”?
a: Eggs are taken, hatched and the young released later
Adult kiwis are sent to zoos around the world
Nests are watched with cameras for poachers
11008.e: Endangered eggs or chicks are taken from the wild and raised in safety. Only when the young are big enough are they released again; this way about 65 per cent reach adulthood.
11008.m: Operation Nest Egg raises young kiwis in safety.

11009.q: Where does the name “kiwi” come from?
a: From Māori, imitating the bird's call
From the name of a sailor
11009.e: The Māori word “kiwi” is thought to be onomatopoeic and imitates the bird's call. Some linguists also link it to Polynesian bird names.
11009.m: The kiwi is named after its own call.

11010.q: At what time of day is the kiwi usually active?
11010.e: Kiwis are mainly nocturnal and spend the day in burrows or thick undergrowth. In predator-free sanctuaries they sometimes come out during the day too.
11010.m: The kiwi is a night bird.

11011.q: What does the kiwi mainly feed on?
a: Invertebrates such as earthworms and insect larvae
11011.e: Kiwis probe the ground with their long bill for earthworms, beetle larvae and other invertebrates. They also eat berries and seeds.
11011.m: The kiwi mainly eats worms and larvae.

11012.q: Apart from smell, what does the kiwi use to find prey in the ground?
a: Touch-sensitive organs in pits at the tip of its bill
11012.e: At the tip of the kiwi's bill there are many small pits with touch receptors. With them, it can sense the vibrations of prey animals in the ground.
11012.m: The kiwi feels for its prey with the tip of its bill.

11013.q: Which structure on the kiwi's head is reminiscent of a cat's whiskers?
a: Long, bristly feathers at the base of the bill
A fleshy comb on the head
Flaps of skin below the bill
11013.e: On its face and around the base of its bill, the kiwi has long, bristle-like feathers. They probably help it feel its way in the dark.
11013.m: The kiwi has feeling bristles like a cat.

11014.q: Roughly what share of a kiwi's body weight is made up of its legs?
11014.e: The strong, marrow-filled legs make up around a third of the body weight. The kiwi is a good runner and digger.
11014.m: The legs make up a third of the kiwi.

11015.q: Which sex of kiwi is usually bigger and heavier?
a: That depends only on the season
11015.e: In kiwis, the females are bigger than the males. In the great spotted kiwi, females weigh up to about 3.3 kg, males only up to about 2.6 kg.
11015.m: In kiwis, the female is the bigger animal.

11016.q: Which zoo was the first in the world to keep a kiwi, from 1851?
11016.e: From 1851, London Zoo was the first zoo in the world to show a kiwi.
11016.m: The first zoo kiwi lived in London from 1851.

11017.q: How do many zoos show kiwis to their visitors?
a: In darkened night houses with a reversed day and night rhythm
11017.e: Kiwis are nocturnal. In night houses it is made dark during the day so that the birds are active when visitors come.
11017.m: In zoos, kiwis are shown in night houses.

11018.q: Which New Zealand coin has shown a kiwi since 1991?
11018.e: Since 1991, the New Zealand one-dollar coin has shown a kiwi. The bird is New Zealand's unofficial national symbol.
11018.m: The kiwi appears on the New Zealand dollar coin.

11019.q: What is the “Bulford Kiwi” in England?
a: A giant chalk picture of a kiwi on a hill
A kiwi that was released into an English park
A stuffed kiwi in the natural history museum
A breed of kiwi raised in England
11019.e: New Zealand soldiers who were waiting near Bulford in 1919 to travel home after the First World War cut a giant kiwi into a chalk hill. The figure still reminds people of them today.
11019.m: The Bulford Kiwi is a chalk figure made by New Zealand soldiers in 1919.

11020.q: Which group of birds does the ostrich belong to?
11020.e: The ostrich is a flightless ratite and, like the emu, rhea, cassowary and kiwi, belongs to the palaeognaths (Palaeognathae).
11020.m: The ostrich is one of the flightless ratites.

11021.q: What is the name of the genus the ostrich belongs to?
11021.e: All living ostriches belong to the genus Struthio. Rhea are rheas, Dromaius emus and Casuarius cassowaries.

11022.q: What does Struthio camelus, the scientific name of the common ostrich, roughly mean?
11022.e: The ancient Greeks called the ostrich “strouthokamelos”, meaning camel sparrow. This became the scientific name Struthio camelus.
11022.m: The ostrich carries the name camel sparrow in its scientific name.

11023.q: Which second ostrich species is today usually recognised as separate, alongside the common ostrich?
11023.e: Since 2014, BirdLife International has listed the Somali ostrich (Struthio molybdophanes) as a separate species. The Masai and Arabian ostriches are subspecies of the common ostrich.
11023.m: The Somali ostrich is now considered a separate ostrich species.

11024.q: What colour is the skin on the neck and thighs of the male Somali ostrich?
11024.e: In the Somali ostrich, the neck and thighs are blue-grey, and a stronger blue in the male during the breeding season. In the North African and Masai ostriches, however, this skin is pink to reddish.
11024.m: You can recognise the Somali ostrich by its blue-grey neck.

11025.q: How is the common ostrich classified on the IUCN Red List?
11025.e: The common ostrich has a huge range and is still common in East Africa, so it is considered not threatened. In some regions, such as West Africa, it has become rare.
11025.m: The common ostrich is considered not threatened worldwide.

11026.q: How does the IUCN classify the Somali ostrich?
11026.e: The Somali ostrich is considered vulnerable. In the Horn of Africa, it is heavily hunted for meat, eggs and medicines.
11026.m: The Somali ostrich is a vulnerable species.

11027.q: When did the last known wild Arabian ostrich die?
11027.e: The Arabian ostrich, a subspecies of the common ostrich, was wiped out by hunting. The last wild bird died around 1966 in Jordan.
11027.m: The Arabian ostrich has been extinct since the 1960s.

11028.q: How many toes does an ostrich have on each foot?
11028.e: The ostrich is the only living bird with just two toes on each foot. This saves weight and helps it run fast.
11028.m: The ostrich is the only bird that runs on two toes.

11029.q: Roughly what is the diameter of an ostrich's eye?
11029.e: At around 5 cm across, the ostrich has the largest eyes of all land vertebrates. This lets it spot enemies from a great distance.
11029.m: The ostrich has the largest eyes of all land animals.

11030.q: Roughly what top speed can an ostrich reach in a sprint?
11030.e: Ostriches can briefly reach around 70 km/h. This makes them the fastest birds on foot.
11030.m: The ostrich is the fastest runner among birds.

11031.q: How long can a single stride of an ostrich be at full speed?
11031.e: With its long legs, the ostrich covers around 3 to 5 m with each stride at high speed.
11031.m: The ostrich covers several metres in one stride.

11032.q: How tall can an adult male ostrich grow?
11032.e: Male ostriches usually grow up to about 2.5 m tall; some sources even give up to 2.75 m. This makes the ostrich the largest living bird.
11032.m: The ostrich is the largest bird in the world.

11033.q: How heavy is an adult male ostrich usually?
11033.e: Male ostriches usually weigh 100 to 130 kg, exceptional birds over 150 kg. No other living bird is heavier.
11033.m: The ostrich is also the heaviest bird in the world.

11034.q: What colour is the plumage of an adult male ostrich?
a: Black with white wing and tail feathers
All white with a black tail
11034.e: The male is black, with white flight feathers and tail. The female, on the other hand, is a plain grey-brown.
11034.m: The male ostrich wears black and white plumage.

11035.q: Why does the female ostrich have grey-brown plumage?
a: She incubates during the day and is well camouflaged
She spends the night in trees
She hunts small animals from an ambush
11035.e: The female sits on the eggs during the day. Her earth-coloured plumage camouflages her on the sandy ground.
11035.m: The brown female ostrich is well camouflaged while incubating during the day.

11036.q: Who incubates the ostrich eggs at night?
a: Nobody, the eggs are left alone
11036.e: During the day the grey-brown main female incubates; at night the black male takes over. His dark colour does not stand out in the dark.
11036.m: In ostriches, the black male incubates at night.

11037.q: How heavy is an ostrich egg on average?
11037.e: An ostrich egg usually weighs around 1.4 kg, some almost 2 kg. That is about the same as 20 to 24 hen's eggs.
11037.m: An ostrich egg weighs as much as about two dozen hen's eggs.

11038.q: What is special about the ostrich egg compared with the size of the bird?
a: Relative to the bird it is one of the smallest bird eggs
Relative to the bird it is the largest bird egg
Relative to the bird it is bigger than a kiwi egg
Relative to the bird it is the same size as a hen's egg
11038.e: In absolute terms, the ostrich egg is one of the largest eggs, but measured against the mother's body it is one of the smallest. In the kiwi, the egg is huge relative to the bird.
11038.m: The ostrich egg is huge in absolute terms but small compared with the female.

11039.q: Roughly how thick is the shell of an ostrich egg?
11039.e: The shell is around 2 to 3 mm thick and very strong. This keeps the embryo well protected during the long incubation.
11039.m: The ostrich eggshell is thick and very tough.

11040.q: Roughly how long is the ostrich's incubation period?
11040.e: The chicks hatch after about 35 to 45 days, so around six weeks.
11040.m: An ostrich chick hatches after about six weeks.

11041.q: What does the main female ostrich do when there are too many eggs in the shared nest?
a: She pushes surplus eggs of other females to the edge
She eats all the other females' eggs straight away
11041.e: An ostrich can only cover about 20 eggs. The main female recognises her own eggs and pushes surplus eggs of other females to the edge.
11041.m: The female ostrich protects her own eggs by sorting out the others.

11042.q: What does an ostrich nest look like?
a: A shallow pit in the ground
A nest of branches in a tree
A hole in a rock face
11042.e: The male scrapes a shallow hollow about 3 m across in the ground. The eggs of the whole harem lie in it.
11042.m: The ostrich nests in a hollow in the ground.

11043.q: What does an incubating ostrich do when in danger, which led to the myth of the “head in the sand”?
a: It lays its neck and head flat on the ground
It really buries its head in the sand
It hides its head under its wing
It plays dead and falls over
11043.e: When in danger, incubating ostriches press themselves flat on the ground. From a distance, it looks as if the head is stuck in the sand.
11043.m: The ostrich does not bury its head in the sand but makes itself flat.

11044.q: What is special about the ostrich's wings compared with those of almost all other living birds?
a: They have claws on the fingers
They are longer than the legs
They can be rolled up completely
11044.e: The ostrich has two to three claws on the fingers of each wing. Most other birds have no such claws at all; only a few, like the rhea or emu, also have one.
11044.m: The ostrich has claws on its wings.

11045.q: What does the ostrich use its wings for, even though it cannot fly?
a: For steering and braking while running
11045.e: When running, the wings act as a rudder and help with sharp turns and braking. It also needs them for courtship and to shade its chicks from the sun.
11045.m: The ostrich steers with its wings when running fast.

11046.q: Why can an ostrich not fly, even though it has wings?
a: Its breastbone has no keel for large flight muscles
It has no bones in its wings
Its feathers are too heavy and hard
Its wings are fused to its body
11046.e: Ratites lack the breastbone keel to which the strong flight muscles attach in flying birds. On top of that, the ostrich is far too heavy to fly.
11046.m: The ostrich lacks the breastbone keel for flight muscles.

11047.q: Why are the ostrich's feathers so soft and fluffy?
a: The barbs lack the tiny hooks that link them
They are made of hair instead of keratin
They are grown new every day
They are filled with water inside
11047.e: In ostrich feathers, the barbs do not hook into each other. So they do not form a firm surface as in flying birds.
11047.m: Ostrich feathers are loose because they lack the hooks.

11048.q: What does the ostrich mainly feed on?
a: Plants such as grasses, seeds and leaves
11048.e: The ostrich mostly eats parts of plants. It only occasionally takes insects, small lizards or rodents as extras.
11048.m: The ostrich is mainly a plant eater.

11049.q: Why does the ostrich swallow stones?
a: To grind up food in its gizzard
To be heavier and stand more steadily
To get minerals for its feathers
To kill parasites in its gut
11049.e: The ostrich has no teeth. Swallowed stones (gastroliths) grind up the tough plant food in the gizzard.
11049.m: The ostrich grinds its food with swallowed stones.

11050.q: Roughly how much can an ostrich's gizzard hold?
11050.e: The gizzard holds up to about 1.3 kg. Up to 45 per cent of that can be sand and stones.
11050.m: There is a lot of sand and stone in an ostrich's gizzard.

11051.q: How does the ostrich get a large part of its water in dry areas?
a: Through dew it licks off its feathers
Through its skin when sand bathing
Through water stored in its crop
11051.e: The ostrich covers much of its water needs with juicy plants and can go several days without drinking. It can even cope with losing up to a quarter of its body weight through drying out.
11051.m: The ostrich gets a large part of its water from its food.

11052.q: What is special about how the ostrich gets rid of waste compared with most other birds?
a: It passes urine and droppings separately
It gets rid of salt through its eyes
11052.e: Unlike most birds, the ostrich passes urine and droppings separately. It collects the urine in an enlarged chamber of the cloaca.
11052.m: The ostrich passes urine and droppings separately.

11053.q: How many females typically belong to the harem of a male ostrich?
11053.e: A male defends a territory and has a harem of usually 2 to 7 females. One of them is the main female.
11053.m: A male ostrich lives together with several females.

11054.q: How does a male ostrich draw attention to himself during courtship and territorial disputes?
a: With loud whistling like a blackbird
With bill clattering like a stork
By drumming his feet on wood
11054.e: The male puffs up his neck and gives a deep, booming call. It sounds similar to a lion's roar.
11054.m: The male ostrich roars almost like a lion.

11055.q: Roughly how long do newly hatched ostrich chicks stay in the nest?
11055.e: Ostrich chicks leave the nest early. After only around three days they leave the nest with their parents.
11055.m: Ostrich chicks leave the nest early.

11056.q: What can happen to the chicks of other ostrich pairs?
a: A strong pair takes them over and leads a large group of chicks
They are always rejected by their parents
They are eaten by the males
They are left alone in the nest
11056.e: When families meet, the dominant pair often takes over the other chicks. This creates groups with dozens or even hundreds of young.
11056.m: Strong ostrich pairs also look after other pairs' chicks.

11057.q: Roughly how big is a young ostrich at one year old?
a: About as big as its parents
About as big as a chicken
About half as big as its parents
About as big as a pigeon
11057.e: Ostrich chicks grow extremely fast. At about one year they reach their parents' height, and their full weight at around 18 months.
11057.m: An ostrich is almost fully grown after just one year.

11058.q: Roughly how many ostrich chicks survive their first year of life?
11058.e: Many chicks are caught by predators and birds of prey. Only around 15 per cent reach the age of one year.
11058.m: Only a few ostrich chicks survive their first year.

11059.q: At what age are ostriches old enough to breed?
11059.e: Females are old enough to breed at about two years, males often only at three to four years. So the females become adult a little earlier.
11059.m: Female ostriches can breed earlier than males.

11060.q: Which weapon does an ostrich use against predators?
a: Powerful forward kicks with its claws
11060.e: Ostriches kick forwards with great force. The claw of the large toe, up to 10 cm long, can even seriously injure lions.
11060.m: An ostrich's kick can be deadly.

11061.q: Which enemies are most dangerous for adult ostriches?
11061.e: Adult ostriches are hunted mainly by big cats, and less often by hyenas and African wild dogs. Eggs and chicks also fall victim to jackals and vultures.
11061.m: Big cats are the ostrich's main enemies.

11062.q: Where does the common ostrich live naturally today?
a: Mainly in Africa south of the Sahara
In the forests of South-East Asia
11062.e: Today the ostrich lives mainly in the savannahs and semi-deserts of Africa south of the Sahara. It used to live in North Africa and western Asia too.
11062.m: Today the ostrich is a bird of the African savannahs.

11063.q: Where does the Somali ostrich live?
11063.e: The Somali ostrich lives in Somalia, north-eastern Ethiopia, parts of Kenya and Djibouti. It prefers bushier land than the common ostrich.
11063.m: The Somali ostrich is a bird of the Horn of Africa.

11064.q: Which ratite from South America is a relative of the ostrich?
11064.e: The rhea lives in South America. The emu and cassowary come from Australia and New Guinea, the kiwi from New Zealand.
11064.m: The rhea is the ostrich's South American relative.

11065.q: What were ostriches especially heavily hunted for in the 18th and 19th centuries?
a: For their feathers as fashion decoration
For their fat as lamp oil
11065.e: Ostrich feathers were very popular on hats and dresses. Hunting almost wiped out the ostrich in parts of North Africa and western Asia.
11065.m: The fashion for feathers nearly wiped out the ostrich.

11066.q: Which town in South Africa is world-famous for its ostrich farms?
11066.e: Oudtshoorn in the Western Cape province became rich through the feather boom and is still the centre of ostrich farming today. South Africa holds a large share of the world market.
11066.m: Oudtshoorn is the capital of ostrich farming.

11067.q: What are ostriches mainly farmed for today?
11067.e: Today, meat and the grainy ostrich leather are the main products. Feathers play only a small role economically.
11067.m: Today ostriches are mainly kept for meat and leather.

11068.q: In which area of Zurich Zoo do ostriches live?
a: In the Kaeng Krachan Elephant Park
11068.e: The Lewa Savanna at Zurich Zoo shows an East African landscape. Ostriches live there together with giraffes, zebras and rhinos.
11068.m: At Zurich Zoo, ostriches live in the Lewa Savanna.

11069.q: How old can ostriches live to in human care?
11069.e: In the wild, ostriches live to about 30 to 40 years. In zoos, some individuals have lived to over 60.
11069.m: An ostrich can live for half a century.

11070.q: What does Aptenodytes, the emperor penguin's genus name, mean?
11070.e: Aptenodytes comes from Ancient Greek and means roughly “wingless diver”. This fits, because the wings have become flippers.

11071.q: The emperor penguin's scientific name is Aptenodytes forsteri, after the naturalist Johann Reinhold Forster. Whose voyage around the world was Forster on?
11071.e: Forster went with James Cook on his second voyage around the world (1772 to 1775), which pushed far to the south. He was probably one of the first people to see emperor penguins.
11071.m: The species name forsteri honours a companion of James Cook.

11072.q: What does “Gray, 1844” after the scientific name Aptenodytes forsteri mean?
a: Who first described the species and in which year
Where the first colony was discovered and how high it lies
Who kept the first emperor penguin in a zoo and when
What colour and weight the first bird had
11072.e: A scientific species name is often followed by the name of the person who first described it and the year. The British zoologist George Robert Gray described the emperor penguin in 1844.
11072.m: The species name is followed by the first describer and the year.

11073.q: Which living species is the only other one in the emperor penguin's genus?
11073.e: Today the genus Aptenodytes includes only the emperor and king penguins. Both are large and have yellow-orange markings on their heads.
11073.m: The emperor and king penguins together make up the genus Aptenodytes.

11074.q: What status has the emperor penguin had on the IUCN Red List since April 2026?
11074.e: In April 2026, the IUCN moved the emperor penguin up from “Near Threatened” to “Endangered”. The main reason is the loss of sea ice due to climate change.
11074.m: The emperor penguin has been considered endangered since 2026.

11075.q: Under which US law was the emperor penguin listed as “threatened” in 2022?
11075.e: The US Fish and Wildlife Service listed the emperor penguin under the Endangered Species Act in October 2022. The rule came into force in November 2022.
11075.m: The USA has protected the emperor penguin as a threatened species since 2022.

11076.q: What is considered the main threat to the emperor penguin?
a: Loss of sea ice due to climate change
Being pushed out by king penguins
11076.e: Emperor penguins need stable sea ice for breeding and moulting. If the ice breaks up too early, chicks that do not yet have waterproof feathers drown or freeze to death.
11076.m: Without stable sea ice, the emperor penguin cannot breed successfully.

11077.q: What is the deepest dive ever measured for an emperor penguin?
11077.e: The record dive of an emperor penguin in 1994 went to a depth of around 564 m. It dives deeper than any other bird.
11077.m: The emperor penguin dives over 500 m deep and holds the bird record.

11078.q: To roughly how many beats per minute can an emperor penguin's heart rate drop when diving?
11078.e: When diving, the emperor penguin slows its heartbeat sharply to about 15 to 20 beats per minute. This saves oxygen and lets it stay under water longer.
11078.m: When diving, the emperor penguin's heart beats very slowly.

11079.q: Roughly how heavy are adult emperor penguins, depending on the season?
11079.e: Adult emperor penguins weigh about 22 to 45 kg. They are heaviest before the breeding season and lightest after fasting.
11079.m: The emperor penguin's weight changes a lot with the seasons.

11080.q: Where does the emperor penguin rank among the heaviest living birds?
11080.e: Only a few ratites such as the ostrich, emu and cassowaries are heavier than the emperor penguin. This puts it in fifth place.
11080.m: Only four living bird species are heavier than the emperor penguin.

11081.q: Roughly how heavy is an emperor penguin's egg?
11081.e: An emperor penguin egg weighs about 450 to 470 g. That is only around 2 to 3 per cent of the mother's body weight.
11081.m: The emperor penguin's egg weighs almost half a kilo.

11082.q: Roughly how long is the emperor penguin egg incubated before it hatches?
11082.e: The egg is incubated for about 65 to 75 days, so just over two months. This is one of the longest incubation periods among birds.
11082.m: An emperor penguin egg is incubated for just over two months.

11083.q: Where does an incubating emperor penguin keep the egg?
a: On its feet under a fold of belly skin
11083.e: Emperor penguins do not build a nest. The egg rests on the feet and is covered by a feathered fold of skin on the belly with a good blood supply.
11083.m: The emperor penguin incubates its egg on its feet.

11084.q: In which months do female emperor penguins usually lay their egg?
11084.e: The egg is laid in May or early June, in the Antarctic winter. The emperor penguin is the only penguin species that breeds in the middle of the Antarctic winter.
11084.m: The emperor penguin breeds in the dark Antarctic winter.

11085.q: On what surface are most emperor penguin breeding colonies?
11085.e: Most colonies are on fast ice, meaning sea ice that is firmly attached to the coast. It has to stay stable until the end of the year.
11085.m: Emperor penguins mostly breed on solid sea ice.

11086.q: Roughly how long does an emperor penguin egg survive if it falls onto bare ice in freezing conditions?
11086.e: At temperatures far below zero, the egg cools down very quickly on the ice. After just one to two minutes the embryo dies.
11086.m: An emperor penguin egg must hardly touch the ice.

11087.q: How much body weight can a male emperor penguin lose between arriving at the colony and his partner returning?
11087.e: During this time the male lives on his fat reserves. He can go down from around 38 kg to about 18 kg.
11087.m: An incubating male emperor penguin loses almost half his weight.

11088.q: What does an emperor penguin father feed his chick if it hatches before the mother returns?
a: A protein-rich secretion from his gullet
Fish saved up in his stomach
11088.e: The father produces a milk-like secretion in his gullet that is rich in protein and fat. With it he bridges a few days until the mother comes back with food.
11088.m: The emperor penguin father can feed his chick a kind of milk.

11089.q: When do female emperor penguins usually return from the sea to the colony?
a: Around hatching time in July and August
11089.e: After laying, the females go off to find food for around two months. They return from about mid-July to early August, when the chicks hatch.
11089.m: The emperor penguin mother comes back for the hatching.

11090.q: What are the groups called that older emperor penguin chicks form while both parents are fishing?
11090.e: About six to seven weeks after hatching, the chicks form large groups called crèches or nurseries. There they are better protected from the cold and from enemies.
11090.m: Young emperor penguins wait for their parents in a nursery.

11091.q: What does the downy coat of an emperor penguin chick look like?
a: Silver-grey with a black head and white face mask
All brown like a king penguin chick
Black with a yellow breast patch
11091.e: Emperor penguin chicks have silver-grey down. The black head with its striking white face mask is typical.
11091.m: The emperor penguin chick wears a white face mask.

11092.q: How far do emperor penguins often walk across the sea ice to their breeding colonies?
11092.e: Because the colonies are far from open water, the birds often march 50 to over 100 km across the ice. They waddle or slide on their bellies.
11092.m: The way to the colony is a long march for the emperor penguin.

11093.q: What temperature can be reached inside a tight huddle of emperor penguins?
11093.e: In the centre of a tight huddle, temperatures of over 20 °C have been measured, while outside it can be far below minus 30 °C.
11093.m: In the middle of an emperor penguin huddle it is surprisingly warm.

11094.q: By roughly how much can emperor penguins reduce their heat loss by huddling together?
a: By up to around 50 per cent
11094.e: In a tight huddle, the bodies shield each other from wind and cold. According to the Australian Antarctic Division, this cuts heat loss by up to half.
11094.m: In a huddle, the emperor penguin saves up to half its heat.

11095.q: What happens to the position of individual emperor penguins within a huddle?
a: The birds take turns between the warm middle and the cold edge
The strongest birds always stay in the middle
The females always stand on the outside
Each bird keeps its place for weeks
11095.e: The huddle is constantly moving. Birds on the cold edge facing the wind move inwards, while others are pushed outwards.
11095.m: In an emperor penguin huddle, everyone gets a turn in the middle.

11096.q: Which principle stops an emperor penguin's feet from losing a lot of body heat?
a: The countercurrent principle in the blood vessels
A thick horny layer with no blood vessels
A 10 cm layer of fat under the soles
11096.e: Arteries and veins lie close together. The warm blood going to the foot gives off heat to the cold blood flowing back, so the heat stays in the body.
11096.m: The countercurrent principle keeps heat in the emperor penguin's body.

11097.q: How does the emperor penguin save heat when breathing out?
a: Special nasal chambers recover the heat from the breath
It breathes only through its mouth
It holds its breath for hours in the cold
Its lungs are wrapped in fat
11097.e: In the nasal chambers, the warm, moist air being breathed out is cooled down. In this way the body gets back a large part of the heat and moisture.
11097.m: The emperor penguin's nose recovers heat.

11098.q: Roughly what share of the emperor penguin's insulation comes from its plumage?
11098.e: The thick, multi-layered plumage provides most of the insulation. The rest comes from a layer of fat under the skin up to 3 cm thick.
11098.m: In the emperor penguin, the plumage does most of the insulating.

11099.q: Why does an emperor penguin stay on land or on the ice during its moult?
a: Its plumage is not waterproof then
It has to incubate during this time
11099.e: During the moult, all the feathers are replaced, which takes about a month. During this time, the bird is not waterproof and fasts.
11099.m: During the moult, the emperor penguin cannot go into the water.

11100.q: Which fish is one of the most important prey species of the emperor penguin?
11100.e: The Antarctic silverfish (Pleuragramma antarctica) often makes up most of its diet. The emperor penguin also eats krill and squid.
11100.m: Silverfish is a main dish of the emperor penguin.

11101.q: Roughly how much food does an adult emperor penguin eat on a normal day?
11101.e: An adult normally eats 2 to 3 kg a day. Before breeding or moulting, when it builds up reserves, it can be up to 6 kg.
11101.m: An emperor penguin eats several kilos of food every day.

11102.q: Which seal hunts emperor penguins, especially as they get in and out of the water at the ice edge?
11102.e: The leopard seal lies in wait at the edge of the ice and catches adult emperor penguins and fledged young. Out at sea, orcas hunt them too.
11102.m: The leopard seal is a dangerous hunter of emperor penguins.

11103.q: Which bird causes more than a third of emperor penguin chick losses in some colonies?
11103.e: Southern giant petrels attack chicks and are responsible for over a third of deaths in some colonies. Skuas, on the other hand, mainly eat dead chicks.
11103.m: The giant petrel is the biggest enemy of emperor penguin chicks.

11104.q: How old do emperor penguins typically live to in the wild?
11104.e: Most emperor penguins live to about 20. Some individuals, however, can reach up to 50 years.
11104.m: An emperor penguin usually lives for about twenty years.

11105.q: Roughly what is the yearly survival rate of adult emperor penguins?
11105.e: Once an emperor penguin has reached adulthood, it has about a 95 per cent chance of surviving each year. The first years of life are the most dangerous.
11105.m: Adult emperor penguins survive almost every year.

11106.q: According to studies, roughly what share of emperor penguin chicks survive their first year?
11106.e: Only about 19 per cent of chicks reach one year of age. Cold, hunger, enemies and ice that breaks up too early claim many victims.
11106.m: Only a few emperor penguin chicks survive their first year.

11107.q: Roughly how many emperor penguin breeding colonies are known today?
11107.e: Thanks to satellite images, the number of known colonies rose from 46 to around 66. They are spread around Antarctica.
11107.m: There are about sixty emperor penguin colonies around Antarctica.

11108.q: How do researchers spot emperor penguin colonies on satellite images?
a: By brown patches of droppings on the ice
By holes in the sea ice
11108.e: The birds' droppings (guano) stain the ice reddish brown. These stains are easy to see from space and give away where the colonies are.
11108.m: Droppings give away emperor penguin colonies from space.

11109.q: According to estimates, roughly how many emperor penguins live worldwide?
11109.e: A worldwide count using satellite images in 2009 found around 595,000 adult birds, which is about a quarter of a million breeding pairs. Since then the population has been falling.
11109.m: There are only a few hundred thousand emperor penguins worldwide.

11110.q: What happened from 2016 in the large emperor penguin colony at Halley Bay?
a: Breeding failed three years in a row
It became the largest colony in the world
It was taken over by king penguins
11110.e: Because the sea ice broke up too early, practically no chicks survived there for three years from 2016. Many birds later moved to the nearby Dawson-Lambton colony.
11110.m: At Halley Bay, the emperor penguins lost their young for three years.

11111.q: Near which island is the northernmost known emperor penguin breeding colony?
11111.e: The colony near Snow Hill Island, close to the Antarctic Peninsula, is considered the northernmost. It is particularly at risk from the warming in this area.
11111.m: The northernmost emperor penguin colony is near Snow Hill.

11112.q: What did three members of Scott's expedition want to collect at Cape Crozier in 1911 on “the worst journey in the world”?
a: Water samples from under the ice
11112.e: Wilson, Bowers and Cherry-Garrard marched to the colony at Cape Crozier in the Antarctic winter to study emperor penguin embryos. Cherry-Garrard described the trip in the book “The Worst Journey in the World”.
11112.m: For three emperor penguin eggs, explorers risked a winter march in 1911.

11113.q: Which documentary about emperor penguins won the Oscar in 2006?
11113.e: The French film “March of the Penguins” by Luc Jacquet shows the breeding cycle of emperor penguins. In 2006 it won the Oscar for Best Documentary.
11113.m: “March of the Penguins” made the emperor penguin world-famous.

11114.q: Where did a lost young emperor penguin, which became famous as “Happy Feet”, turn up in 2011?
11114.e: The young emperor penguin got stranded on a beach in New Zealand in 2011 and ate sand, which it probably mistook for snow. It was cared for and later released into the Southern Ocean.
11114.m: “Happy Feet” was an emperor penguin that swam all the way to New Zealand.

11115.q: How do emperor penguin partners and chicks recognise each other in the noisy colony?
a: By individual calls with two voices at once
By the smell of their feathers
By the shape of their bill
11115.e: Emperor penguins have no fixed nests. Their calls are made with two voices at the same time, and the beats between them produce an unmistakable pattern.
11115.m: The emperor penguin recognises its family by its voice.

11116.q: According to studies, how often does a pair of emperor penguins breed together again the following year?
a: Only in around 15 per cent of cases
In around 95 per cent of cases
In around 60 per cent of cases
11116.e: Emperor penguins stay with one partner only within a breeding season. Only about 15 per cent of pairs get back together the following year.
11116.m: Emperor penguins look for a new partner almost every year.

11117.q: How are the emperor penguin's bones different from those of most flying birds?
a: They are solid and not hollow
They are partly made of cartilage
11117.e: Like all penguins, the emperor penguin has dense, heavy bones. This reduces buoyancy and makes diving easier.
11117.m: Heavy bones help the emperor penguin dive.

11118.q: How fast does an emperor penguin swim on average when looking for food?
11118.e: When looking for food, the emperor penguin usually moves at 6 to 9 km/h. In short sprints it is much faster.
11118.m: The emperor penguin swims at a leisurely pace when looking for food.

11119.q: What is special about the emperor penguin's social behaviour compared with other penguin species?
a: It does not defend a territory
11119.e: The emperor penguin is the only penguin species without territorial behaviour. This is the only way the birds can huddle tightly together in winter.
11119.m: The emperor penguin has no territory of its own.

11120.q: Which snake family does the king cobra belong to?
11120.e: The king cobra is an elapid from the family Elapidae. This family also includes cobras, mambas, kraits and coral snakes.
11120.m: The king cobra belongs to the elapid family.

11121.q: What does Ophiophagus, the king cobra's genus name, mean?
11121.e: Ophiophagus is made up of the Greek “ophis” for snake and “phagein” for to eat. The name describes its main food, other snakes.

11122.q: In which region of the world do king cobras live?
a: In Africa south of the Sahara
11122.e: King cobras live from India through southern China and Indochina to the Philippines and Indonesia. Since 2024, four species have been recognised there.
11122.m: The king cobra lives in South and South-East Asia.

11123.q: In zoological naming, what applies when a genus name has already been given to other animals?
a: The group named later needs a new name
The larger group of animals gets it
You simply add a number to the name
11123.e: Each genus name may only be valid once in the animal kingdom. The king cobra was first called Hamadryas, but the name was already taken by butterflies, so today it is called Ophiophagus.
11123.m: A genus name may only occur once in the animal kingdom.

12474.q: How many eyes does a tarantula have?
12474.e: Tarantulas have eight small eyes, usually arranged in two rows on a little mound. They see poorly and rely mainly on touch and vibrations.
12474.m: Despite eight eyes, a tarantula sees poorly.

12870.q: What did the Earth form from?
12870.e: Dust and lumps of rock were circling in space. They crashed into each other and stuck together into bigger and bigger lumps until the Earth was formed.
12870.m: The Earth formed from dust and rock circling in space.

12871.e: The Sun formed first. Then the planets, including the Earth, formed from what was left around the Sun.
12871.m: The Sun is older than the Earth.

12872.q: What was the Earth like at the very beginning?
12872.e: The young Earth was so hot that its rock glowed and was liquid. Only slowly did it cool down.
12872.m: The young Earth was glowing hot.

12873.e: Lava is rock that is so hot it becomes liquid. It comes out of the Earth at volcanoes.
12873.m: Lava is liquid, glowing hot rock.

12874.q: According to scientists today, how was the Moon formed?
12874.e: Scientists think that a large body in space crashed into the young Earth. The Moon formed from the debris.
12874.m: The Moon probably formed after a big collision with the Earth.

12875.q: Where did the first life on Earth appear?
12875.e: Scientists think that the first living things appeared in water. The water probably protected them from the Sun’s dangerous rays.
12875.m: The first life probably appeared in water.

12876.q: How big were the first living things?
12876.e: The first living things were so small that you can only see them with a microscope. They were single-celled organisms like bacteria.
12876.m: The first living things were tiny single-celled organisms.

12877.q: Which planet is the Earth, counting from the Sun?
12877.e: From the Sun, first come Mercury and Venus, then the Earth. That is why the Earth is the third planet.
12877.m: The Earth is the third planet from the Sun.

12878.e: The Earth is almost as round as a ball. You can see this clearly on photos taken from space.
12878.m: The Earth is almost the shape of a ball.

12879.q: What was there a lot of on the young Earth?
12879.e: On the young Earth volcanoes erupted everywhere. There were no plants or animals yet.
12879.m: There were very many volcanoes on the young Earth.

12880.q: What formed when the Earth slowly cooled down and it rained for a long time?
12880.e: When the Earth cooled down, water vapour turned into rain. The water collected in the low places and formed the seas.
12880.m: When the Earth cooled down, the seas formed.

12881.q: What is it like deep inside the Earth?
12881.e: Inside the Earth it is still very hot today. The deeper you go, the hotter it gets.
12881.m: Inside the Earth it is very hot.

12882.q: What is the centre of the Earth called?
12882.e: Right in the middle of the Earth is the core. It is made mainly of iron.
12882.m: The centre of the Earth is called the core.

12883.q: What is the outermost, solid layer of the Earth that we live on called?
12883.e: The Earth’s crust is the outer, solid layer of the Earth. Compared with the whole Earth it is as thin as the skin of an apple.
12883.m: We live on the Earth’s crust.

12884.q: Who lived on Earth first: fish or dinosaurs?
12884.e: Fish existed long before the dinosaurs. The dinosaurs came much later.
12884.m: Fish existed long before the dinosaurs.

12885.q: Do the continents always stay in the same place?
a: Yes, they are tied to the seabed.
12885.e: The continents move only a few centimetres each year. But over millions of years they travel a long way.
12885.m: The continents move very slowly across the Earth.

12886.q: What was the name of the huge continent at the time of the first dinosaurs, in which almost all land was joined together?
12886.e: More than 200 million years ago, when the first dinosaurs lived, almost all the land on Earth was joined together. This giant continent is called Pangaea.
12886.m: The giant continent Pangaea later broke up into today’s continents.

12887.e: Africa slowly pushed against Europe. The rock was squeezed together and folded upwards, and that is how the Alps were formed.
12887.m: The Alps were formed because rock was pushed together.

12888.q: What do people sometimes find high up in the Swiss Alps?
12888.e: The rock of the Alps used to lie on the seabed. That is why fossilised shells and snails are found up there.
12888.m: Fossilised sea creatures are found in the Alps.

12889.e: The word comes from Greek. “Deinos” means terrible and “sauros” means lizard.

a: They were born alive like calves.
They grew in their mother’s pouch.
12890.e: Dinosaurs laid eggs, just as birds and crocodiles do today. Scientists have found many fossilised dinosaur eggs.

12891.e: Tyrannosaurus rex was a big meat-eater. It had a huge mouth with sharp teeth.

12892.q: What was strikingly small on Tyrannosaurus rex?
12892.e: Tyrannosaurus rex had a huge head and strong legs. But its arms were very short.
12892.m: Tyrannosaurus rex had very short arms.

12893.q: On how many legs did Tyrannosaurus rex walk?
12893.e: Tyrannosaurus rex walked on its two powerful back legs. It kept its balance with its long tail.
12893.m: Tyrannosaurus rex walked on two legs.

12894.q: How many horns did Triceratops have on its face?
12894.e: “Triceratops” means three-horned face. It had two long horns above its eyes and a short one on its nose.
12894.m: Triceratops had three horns on its face.

12895.e: Triceratops was a plant-eater. It used its beak to pluck plants.

12896.q: What was especially long on Brachiosaurus?
12896.e: Brachiosaurus had a very long neck. This let it eat leaves high up in the trees.
12896.m: Brachiosaurus had a very long neck.

12897.q: What did Stegosaurus have on its back?
12897.e: Stegosaurus had a row of large bony plates on its back. On its tail it had sharp spikes.
12897.m: Stegosaurus had large plates on its back.

12898.q: What did Ankylosaurus have at the end of its tail?
12898.e: Ankylosaurus had armour made of bony plates. At the end of its tail it had a heavy club of bone that it could use to defend itself.
12898.m: Ankylosaurus had a bony club on its tail.

12899.q: What did some dinosaurs, for example Velociraptor, have?
12899.e: Scientists have found out that many smaller dinosaurs had feathers. Velociraptor was one of them.

12900.q: Which animals today are descended from dinosaurs?
12900.e: Birds developed from small, feathered dinosaurs. You could say that birds are today’s dinosaurs.

12901.q: What do we call scientists who study dinosaur fossils?
12901.e: Palaeontologists study living things from prehistoric times. They dig up fossils and examine them.

12902.q: How do we know what dinosaurs looked like?
12902.e: Nobody has ever seen a dinosaur. Scientists put fossilised bones together and so find out how the animals were built.
12902.m: Fossilised bones show us what dinosaurs looked like.

12903.q: Did humans and dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus rex live at the same time?
12903.e: Many millions of years lie between the big dinosaurs and the first humans. Films in which people fight dinosaurs are made up.
